blocks.x: I remember when Lawrence had a band. Yeah, that's right. He died right after, remember? Yeah, just two years ago. That's Sam Dutré. Yeah, Sam, yeah. Yeah, that's a good picture. Yeah.
This is when I was with Fredrick Coleman band. Oh yeah. At the Mardi Gras. We worked there three years with Fredrick. You know that the Mardi Gras by Silverville? Yes, I remember.
About next to where I'm at now?
Yeah, I remember.
This is a little trio we had at the Playhouse on Boydman, St. Louis a couple of years ago. Oh yeah. Yeah, Bob Hopton.
Who else is there?
Bob Hopton.

A lot of them. A lot of them. A lot of them. They know a man for a record company. Where was this again, Dave? They used to call it, you know, right? From the 500 Club, they used to call it one time, the Playhouse. Oh.
On Bourbon there?
Yeah, Bourbon in St. Louis. Uh-huh.
Yeah. Let me see, which corner? Was that on the river side over there? Yeah, that's right.
That's right. It's called the Playhouse. Yeah, I seem to remember that.
Is that where the gas part used to be, too, or not?
That's right. That's right. That's a long time ago. Yeah, a long years ago when I first came down here, you said. That's right.
I think Burnell played there once, but I don't know if I ever heard him. I didn't know if I did. Burnell, St. Louis. Burnell, St. Louis.
Long time, right? Might have heard him there once, I didn't know it. He's gonna pick me back up and got tied, sleeping on the piano at the paddock. The paddock.
The paddock. Yeah, the paddock. Yeah, the paddock. Yeah. That's a while back.
Yeah, that's before they had the horses all over the wall and everything, too.
That's right. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.
Oh, yeah. I'll give my front picture, the pad and the Al picture there. Mm-hmm. You ain't all in my perspective to recall it coming, you know. That's all they have.

I'll make a note on the tape here that we're interviewing Mr. Dave Williams at his home, 1901 Milton, isn't it? Up near St. Bernard and the date is July the 2nd, 1961. So, when we go to transcribe this in there, look at what tape it is.

Now, this band you're playing at Leroy's on Burmese Street with, Dave, is that your band? You're leading that band? That's my band, yeah. Uh-huh. And you've got Sam Dutre in there? And who else is in the band with you?
Willie Joss, Josh Willis at least. You know Josh Willis the trumpet man? Uh-huh. And Marvin, Tram Martin, Justin Joss on the drum. And then McNeil Groh was on the bass.
Did you say also Kimball sometimes?
Kimball played banjo sometimes. Yeah, Groh played bass.
We might start out at the beginning of your life, if you can tell us just where you were born. Were you born right here in town?
Yeah, I was born right here in New Orleans. What part of the city? Yeah, right there in the 27th Ward up front of town around, I would say, 1100 block, 2 O'erth Street. Downtown then?
Yeah, 1920. What was your birth date, if you don't mind telling me?
Yeah, it was the 26th of August, 1920. So you're about 40?
I'm 40 right now. You're 41 almost. I'll be 41 in August.
In August, yeah.

Can you tell us anything about the earliest music that you ever heard? Did your parents play anything? Did you hear anything? Oh yeah, my parents, I think I didn't hear it, Bill. But my mother, she played piano until yet she played.
She played organ at the church now. Yeah, the first free-wheel Baptist church, Truro and Claymore. She always did play and had a few great fellas playing piano in my family.
Two Mitchell Frazier.
For him.
I wanted to ask you about your family some more. How you, I knew you were related to the Morello's.
Morello's, that's right. Morello's Morello, yeah. My old Uncle Lawrence.
How are you related? Which is your mother?
I relate to my grandfather's side. Your grandfather? Yeah, so my grandfather and Lawrence's mother are sisters and brothers.
Was he a Marrero then?
No, they married him Marrero. They were Frazers too, I guess. Yeah, that's right. See, my aunt was my grandfather's sister. It was Frazier. And she married Marrero.
So you related two of them in that way?
Yeah, that way, yeah.

Do you remember when you were a boy, it was the old Billy Marrero, Lawrence's father. The old man played the bass, everybody said he was a wonderful musician. Did you get to hear him? Did you remember him?
I never got to hear him. I overheard talk of him.
I forgot when he died.
He died a long time ago. Must have been another dead before. I don't know, I don't remember.
Might have been dead when you were born.
Yeah, yeah.
Did your father play any instruments?
Yeah, my father played a little piano. Yeah, he did too. But he never taken a professional job or anything.
I guess you always had a piano in your home then.
Like something about a catch, you know. He always had a piano at home. My mother really was able. And I liked playing for my mother. Which I was a kid, five years old, playing piano.
You started when you were there?

Yeah, I always did play piano. Now the only lesson I would take was right after I come out to service in 1948, but I went to school on a GI Bill, you know. I learned a little music, not too much. I formed up a couple of bands myself. Like a little company. Tell us a little bit more about when you started out.
Did your mother help you any? Or did you just watch her and learn?

Well, I watched my mother-in-law and she taught me a few notes and I don't know, somehow I just find myself playing. I used to play many, doing little nickel parties all around the neighborhood and things like that.
Did you have a method when you started or learned to read music or just pick it up?
I didn't learn how to read music. I just started playing. Just played.
Did you play tunes? A popular tune? Yeah, popular tunes. I played tunes, yeah. You just picked them out at first?
Just picked them out and just played them, man.
Yeah. Get the chords in the bass and everything? That's right.
Yeah. Yeah, I started with a drummer just piano, you know, me on the piano. And look again, I had a horn. I went on a true time like that with a little four or five pieces or two.
What were these little nickel parties or something for the kids or real things?
Yeah, a nickel party with kids, then the girl people started hybring. Yeah. The girl people started hybring. I played many, many parties.
Is there somebody at the door if you want to see me? Yeah. Sorry, you won't have a minute. We can stop. Somebody wants to see you. What? You say you just used drums at first.
Yeah, drums, you know.
Can you remember when you hit with you on your own drum there?

Oh yeah, I can remember good. The old fellow was quite older than me and he knew how to play a little bit. You know, Brittany brought me around and there was Norman Blaze. Old boy, he died about ten years ago. I never knew him. No, he played much of his dance? He never just got up to himself and made no kind of laugh for himself. Always played a little drum. Well, quite now he was a fellow old enough to be my dad, you know. He liked my playing. He got a few little jobs like that. Then parties went up to diamonds and we were going to play for a little dollar a week, I mean a dollar a night or so like that. And I played, after I got to be a kid, about fifteen years old, then I played a few jobs out on Burger Street. Yeah.
I played fifteen then. Remember these parties, how old were you at the parties?
Playing parties?

Yeah, when you first started out. Yeah, when you first started out. I'll turn it off for a second. You started on Burger Street when you were about fifteen. Was that playing piano by yourself or was it playing piano?
Played a little drum. You remember, you used to call this place the, you know the Dream Room? Yeah. They had another man for it, and Mr. Johnny had it.
Oh yeah, I can't think now. I remember once George Lewis played there for a while and then a band from Dayton, Ohio was now.
That's right.
That was Club Slipper, was it?
Club Slipper.
Club Slipper, was that it?
Club Slipper. But I played Club Slipper, that was quite a while back. And they liked me there.
How old would you be when you were playing these nickel parties then, Dave?
About twelve, fifteen, about fifty years old. Little nickel parties.
Were those just parties in people's homes or were they like fish fries or whatever?

Yeah, they had like fish fries. See like fish fries? Those kind of parties. Then they had little house parties. Picking up nickel at the door, young children come in and dance, buy lemonade cake. And from there I went on, I found myself in a citizen club with about five pieces, playing a dance.
You were always playing for dancing even at these nickel parties, they were still dancing.
Still dancing.
Do any singing?

Oh yeah, I mean I do my own singing. Do any singing. Do any singing? Oh. Then I wired them down that way up. Well I went to the service in 41. I came back out when I started a little band in the service. Yeah, and I played all around Manala, Okinawa, you know, around. You were over in the 70 band. Yeah, I mean they did. My little band was sort of nice and the common commander gave me transportation. But people even hired my little band across C. I mean I had to leave the company, you know, give me time and leave the company. We'd go from Manala to Okinawa.
Yeah.
Kids all sitting, you know, around.
How big a band did you have then?
Oh, I had about seven feet then.
Anybody else from the Oregon's?
A nice band then.
Anybody else from Louisiana or Oregon's?
No, there was one bar from here. And that was Andrew Brown, he played bass. And he's in California now, Andrew Brown. The rest of the fellows from different parts of the state.
Did they, how'd they seem? Did they seem to have the right style to hear? Did they seem the same? Yeah. Did they have good swing and all drums?

Oh, I took plenty of time with them. I know how I did it. I showed them a lot. Some of the boys, one of the fellows, they know anything too much about the instrument. But the drummer was a drummer. A drummer. Yeah. Land was large, brilliant. But we have to have something over there that was so lousy.
Yeah, sure.
You know, so we flew around, flew around, come in command, got some instruments, got in the piano. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. The weather was very hot weather, but plenty of random weather too. We didn't ever have anything to what you live in here. We built everything we lived in, we built by ourselves.
Build up the camp.

Yeah, built up the camp by ourselves. I wouldn't be no special service. I'd come into the service, to the Army. I didn't go into special service. Just playing out for the 590 Ordnance. Ammunition company, the thing was so dead. I always could play piano. I should have went in at special service, but I just didn't know what I was doing. That's how I got hooked in it. I made the best out of that.
You had a piano then at the camp, because you got to play on it.

Oh yeah, yeah. Every time one gets bad, my couple men get better. He got better kicks out of himself. He brought many big parts over, you know. Yeah, but he liked it himself. They get a little awesome too.
Sure, yeah. The music is a couple of awesome.
Well, it's been a long time for you. I bet you were glad to get back, don't you? I bet you got back. I bet you got back.

Well, after I got discharged in the 40th, I came on back to the state. I flew around California for a while. I got discharged out of Fairfield, California. I come on out of St. Louis, Missouri, and I crossed over the river in East St. Louis, Illinois. Yeah. And I was taking a job at a nightclub there, playing piano, or Nick Country Club, they call it. East St. Louis, Illinois. And Randy didn't want me to leave there. And I worked there long. I worked there about eight, nine months. I left. I come on home. I came home. And that's where I went to school. And I joined Fairfield Court.
Were there many other musicians? Probably a few occasionally tell us that they went to that school. I can't remember anybody else in there at the same time you were?

Yeah. Clever Town Hall. That's where I remember you. Clever, you were there. Wendell Eugene. Yeah. Good boy. Seems like a couple other people have told me. A lot of boys. I can't recall that man. It wasn't the one the Sheik was at, was it?
Sheik went through, didn't he?
Sheik, yeah.
Sheik did. Yeah, I knew. That's right.
Sheik went through.
Yeah, Willard Hufford, he was teaching there. The Claudette, Willard Hufford. Who were the other teachers?
Any others that we know of, the jazz musicians that might have been teachers?
I think a few of them you do know. You see, like Willard Hufford or one of your genius teachers. This fella Clyde. Who remember Clyde? He was teaching.
I remember for sure. I was thinking Louie Nelson went to some school, but I think he went to learn something else, he told us. Louie Nelson?
Yeah, trombones.
Trombones? What was that? He was going to, some other trade he learned, I think. I forget what it was. Was that the GI? Yeah, on the GI. He was a mailman, no.
He was a mailman unless he went into that. Yeah, he was.
He was driving a mail truck. I think he had another job.

Something else, some other kind of a trade he learned. I don't think he ever did follow. Anyway, that was right after the war. I guess that lasted a couple of years, so I know, those GI's built. Raymond Burke went to one of them too. A little bit. He never did really learn to read though, even when he went to that. He doesn't like to read.
Although he can read more than he'll admit. Yeah, yeah. That's how he's reading. He gets mixed up on his flats, I'm sure. Sure.
What was your main job then after that? You said that Freddie Coleman, you went with him.
Yeah, I went with Freddie Coleman.
The bunch was in the picture, mostly. Yeah. So you all was there. Tourmalon played with him for a while, didn't he?

Yeah, Tourmalon was with us. He was playing bass, wasn't he? He was playing bass. Well, during that time, I was at the Matty Grind, and this is all the employees here, Joe Robichore. He was playing intermissions. Oh yeah.
That's when Lizzie was there.

Yeah, Joe Robichore and Lindsey Miles. I see, who else? That Lindsey Miles there, there's Joe Robichore sitting beside me at the piano. That one big picture they're taking, all the employees. Let's go from left to right.
Who's this on clarinet?
That was the bar, that's Cindy Davila. Oh yeah, Cindy Davila.

And the trombone behind him? Oh, Wendell Eugene. And there's Willie Humphrey. Willie Humphrey. And this is Lizzie. Lizzie. And who's this on trumpet? Talking about Jefferson. Oh yeah, Thomas Jefferson. That's Thomas Jefferson. That was a wild one.
That's Frederick Coleman himself. And who's on bass? And that's Clement. Clement Camelot. Oh, Clement. He wasn't as heavy then.
Couldn't recognize him hardly. He's pretty light weight.
Yeah, I think that was a nice summer. And Willie Humphrey. And Willie Humphrey. Yeah. Frog was with you there for a while though too. The records they made, I think he...
Frog came there after Wendell left. See, Wendell on Tramble on that night.
After Wendell left and Frog came. Those records that Cook, a fellow from Long Island made, were you on those? I never did have those. They were cut out.

Well, I was on a lot of records. Fred had made a lot of records. Yeah, we did record. And I was wrong, because he's always loved me to try to find it. I still can't find any. I never did hear those records myself. I had them once.
I had Willie Humphrey. Willie Humphrey, somebody bought a copy of it. That's the last copy I ever got. And they didn't have a distributor.
I think the company is perfectly out of business now. At least you can't get that record. I don't know what happened.

Yeah, because this old boy, Smiling Joe, he made some numbers too with us during the time. And you worked with him then on... Oh, I did plenty of work with Smiling Joe. He made some numbers too with us during the time. You worked with him then on...
Oh, I did plenty of work with Smiling Joe. He made some numbers too with us during the time.
You worked with him then on...
I did plenty of work with Smiling Joe. I did plenty of work with him. I really was once... I was a pianist one time and started working by himself.

Yeah, I guess he worked almost all the places along there. I remember anything at the famous door and... Yeah. Did you remember here at the famous door with him? Some place in the dream room or some place along on that side of the street?

Well, we was out when I was playing with him. We worked at Texas Lines. Worked some nice jobs out of town. Plenty of nice jobs. I worked with Smiling Joe out of town. All over Canal Street. Boydman Street and I worked.

I was going to ask about some of the old time pianists, since naturally we're interested in the old history as much as we can find. Yeah. A lot of those fellas are gone now, but there might be some you'd remember. Even people like Bernal San Diego who wasn't so old.
That's right.
Do you remember his playing, what he played like?
Yeah, I remember his playing. I mean, he was one of my all. I mean, I liked him very much. I'm not sure I got to hear him. I don't know.
Some people say he was mostly just a blues player and others say he'd play everything. I don't know.

It's wonderful. Well, Bernal San Diego, I mean, in fact, I've been around with him quite a bit. I mean, he's a man riding on him. He played plenty of piano, plenty of anything. Plenty of blues, plenty of jumpy piano. I mean, he had fast fingers.
That's what I heard.
Fast fingers. Fast fingers I never knew a man of heaven. He never did it. Yeah. And he could play a nice, slow pianist, any type of piano he wanted to play.
Did he work mostly by himself?
He worked mostly by himself. That's the way he worked mostly by himself.
Did you ever hear him in a band? How was he in a band if he ever played in one?
Well, I heard him one time in the band. He just sitting. One night, Count Basie came down there on the gate. I think it was Count Basie. And I told Count Basie, get up and let him play a number.
I guess after Count Basie playing the front finger here, he really made the piano jump.
People wanted to know I was going to play with that band and I would play with it before. But man, that guy got there and made that band jump.
Yeah, it'd be quite a different one.
Yeah, he made that band jump. And during that time now they had some other old piano players like I just mentioned a while back, like Mitchell Frazier. Oh yes, I never heard anything about him.
Great ball.
I think he was during that time, I think he was one of the best. Mitchell Frazier.
How was he related to Sae for instance? Oh, they were related for his cousin.
First cousin. Yeah, him, Sae and my mother, their first cousin. And he got another boy, he's still living, Simon Frazier.

Yeah, Simon, I've heard him play a couple of times. He used to be over playing with Punch a few nights, about four years ago. I haven't seen him since. Oh, another good pianist I missed hearing is, I can't think of it, Lewis, you know, with P-Roll. What's his name?
Steve.
Steve Lewis.
Did you ever hear him, Dave? You miss him, Steve Lewis?

Yeah, you must have heard him. I miss hearing him myself. I would play a talk, I would miss all of them. Never been around, I don't think. Well, that fellow's supposed to be dead, right? Oh, yes, he died.

Oh, he died. He would have been pretty young, I guess, when he died. I see a friend of mine hurt him, though, here in 1938 or 39. 39. I think he died soon after that. You should have been around 20 years old, man. At least. About the time that the war started, then, was he? He probably died during the war, eh?
Well, I think that's what probably happened. See, that made me miss a lot of those fellows, too, you know? Being a young man when that war broke out.
Yeah, then you went away. Yeah.

Yeah, that made me really miss a lot of the poor times. I was just by the stage to be mingling with them, you know? But anyhow, getting around them, anyhow, 19, 20 years old. I knew I was going to start getting around them, because I was very interested in my music, you know? I knew I was going to start getting around them, but I was drafted to the service. Must have been about 19, 20 years old then when I was drafted to the service.

One pianist they talk about, I don't know how long he was around here, Udell Wilson, I think he came from Kansas City. Did you ever hear him? Wilson? Udell Wilson, yeah, he played, oh, in the late, about the time you were born. I guess he was growing strong. I don't know if he stayed here long enough for you to hear him or died. I don't know if he was there.
He was there. I don't remember hearing him. I don't remember. Do you remember the name?
What name would it have been?
Oh, I don't remember.
Somehow you hear about a lot of the girls that played piano, too, all of you today. People like Emma Barrett and Mrs. Kimmel.
Emma, yeah, Emma, Mrs. Kimmel, and the square of fun, isn't it? Who? Uh-uh-uh.

Well, Billy Pierce, of course, there's always been a lot of women here to play the dance. Who's with Tom Shorten? There's Mercedees, I forget, what is her name, Gorman, Mercedees Gorman, does you know her? Is she still around? I've never met her. Not sure.
I think she rhymed with Selty. I don't know, I don't remember, for quite a while she played at a gig. Yeah, I think she played with Punch. Oh, with Punch? Once or twice I heard her with Punch.
Yeah, but I don't know her.
I've been up to her house. She lives uptown somewhere.
That's right, she did.
Did your mother ever play anything except church music?
Well, when she was a little younger, I guess she played around a little bit, but not much. She didn't know how she played. Never played with any bands?

I don't know. I meant to ask you about Bernal Santiago. Did he sing guitar with his, what do you say, worked on his own? No, but I didn't do anything. Didn't do anything, just playing? Just playing. Uh huh. Any of those men we talked about, were any of them singers? No, they didn't do anything. Mitchell, he didn't sing.

No, you know, quite a notch, everybody, he doesn't know soul, you know, so he played down a few words. Yeah, yeah. No, I never thought I was singing, he didn't sing. I wonder if they, uh. They'd take it up like, you know, like I do how I think. I ain't doing nothing unless I open my big mouth. No, it sounds fine. Yeah.
I like your singing. Yeah.
I like your singing. Yeah. I like your singing. Yeah. I like your singing. Yeah. I like your singing.
Yeah. I like your singing. Yeah. I like your singing. I was wondering about any of the old time party pianists.
There's one man we were just thinking about when we drove up here. He has a garage over here, uh, Baby Bruce, they call it. His real name is Bruce.
Bruce, I'm trying to get Bruce, Bruce to his, not all of them. I try to get him away until he comes.

We were over and interviewed him and we told him that sometime we'd like to record him on the piano, maybe up to Tulane or someplace, because he's never made any records. Yeah. He tried a couple, you know that old beat up piano he has in his place over there? Yeah, he's been on that one.
Yeah, we interviewed him there.

He only played a couple of numbers, but the piano had been sitting in the water at that time. Yeah, sitting in the water now? Yeah, very good. Yeah, very good. And we told him we'd be back in about a month and we all stopped to see him anyway. I have a microphone, I have a good microphone. Let's go over there. Bruce, just left him. He just left him a little bit, about ten minutes before you all come.
You see him again, tell him we haven't forgotten him.

I sure will. And then we'll be around to see him some of these days. Yeah, I try to make Bruce wait until you all come. Yeah, he played a few old numbers and he used to play things like China, some blues, some good blues, yeah. What was it, something about Tennessee Woman he called it, one of his favorite blues.
You know you wouldn't believe when they got some of these fellas around him singing and playing a little piano. I think if the people could hear him they'd get a break.
Yeah, he seemed to have a lot of talent. I bet at one time he could really, he still plays a good one. We heard him even on that beat up piano sounded good.
Yeah, he got an old upright mind back there. You know, you're all in the water. I go back there and play some time, got a nice tool to it.
I see your piano has got, it's a whirl line, it says damp proof. Damp proof.
Really? What do they do to it?
I wonder what they do to it. Do you know Dave?
Well, it's a, I tell you the fact, you could mostly see it yourself. The quality of it, you see the wood of it, you see. You don't just see damp proof, the water's going with it.
Do they do anything with the strings maybe?
The hard and heavy, and the strings are big, the strings are thick. Maybe they might be a stainless steel or something. Yeah.

The keys, the keys look good. I mean, they really work good. It's in a good, perfect shape. Yeah, it's in a good shape. Yeah. Did you hear any other old time pianists, say, along that period, like Bruce or any of the others that you can think of, that maybe we haven't heard of, that you ran across in some of those parties, that maybe when you'd be playing they'd come in and sit in or anything. Do you remember any of the earlier ones when you were just a kid, even? Well, I had a few. Some I forgot, and a few of them I think of.
Some of them I really forgot their names. But I remember during the time when I was coming up to this bar, Joe Hopkins, he played nice piano. Hopkins, I don't even know that.
Yeah, Joe Hopkins.
Is he still living you think?
Yeah. Oh yeah. Does he play, he still play, right? Yeah, he still play.
You know where he playing? Right in the corner of the two sisters right now. Oh, on Ronald Street now?
Oh. Oh. But at the Bourbon Street. Yeah, they have a trope on the front street on Bourbon Street.
Oh, yeah, on the Bourbon Street, yeah. Yeah, you know the code two sisters where they can enter? Well, they got a little place right there. Right on the side. Yeah, that's the other one.
Yeah, not where the stroke man, what's his name, Henry?
The old Henry, no, right in the middle of the Henry. Yeah, they call him Joe Hopkins. And he got a brother who plays piano and sings very well. They call him Sam Hopkins.
But is he working there? Sam.
Yeah.
Heee! Saxmo Armstrong, let's have a nice hand. Louie, ladies and gentlemen, and Louie, you know, in just exactly two days, on July 4th, will be Saxmo's 61st birthday.
That's right.

And Louie, on behalf of every American in our country, for all the wonderful things you've done for our country, a very happy birthday and many happy returns of the day. Let's hear it out there. Louie.

Louie, you're welcome. Thank you. Now, the pale moon shining on the fields below. The folks of Groening, soft and low. You need to tell me why, because I know. Good evening, everybody. dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear The End The End The End The End The End The End The End The End Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.
Thank you.

I'm biding my time. Next year, next year, something's bound to happen. This year, this year, I'm going to keep on in that morning biding my time. Oh, cause that's the kind of girl I'm regretting when I'm sitting here biding my time. I want a pack or two of pockets, a true or something, darn on your dad. Just to make me thunder, where the world's a weapon is free. I want a steady water, body my time.

I want a steady water, body my time. Next Sunday night, Ingrid Bergman, Yves Montand, and Tony Perkins. Headline R show in a movie scene from Anatole Litbox, Goodbye Again, which should be a tremendous hit. A love story in which Ingrid Bergman loves Parisian playboy Yves Montand, and is comforted by the youthful Tony Perkins when Montand becomes indifferent. It's distinguished not only by their performances, but by the skillful direction of Anatole Litbox against the colorful backgrounds of Paris. Now, in addition to this star trio of Bergman, Montand, and Perkins, you'll meet Foley's Brigere dancing star Eileen O'Dare, the amazing Gally Gally, you'll enjoy the comedy pyrotechnics of Joey Adams, trying to get a word in edgewise with double-talking Al Kelly, the completely zany Phyllis Diller in some of her Vegas moments, Harlem's Timmy Rogers, Felicia Sanders, and for the youngsters, the unrecording sensations from the Northwest, the Brothers Four. So see you next Sunday with all of these stars, and remember... CBS Television Network programs are pre-recorded today for broadcast of this time zone.

segments.title: Looking at photos: Coleman band at Mardi Gras and the Playhouse trio
segments.summary: Russell and Williams look at photographs: Williams with Freddie Coleman's band at the Mardi Gras and a trio at the Playhouse on Bourbon and St. Louis, with talk of the location and the Paddock.

segments.title: Recording note and Williams's current band at Leroy's
segments.summary: Russell notes the date, place and tape; Williams names the members of his band at Leroy's.

segments.title: Birth in New Orleans, 1920
segments.summary: Williams was born in the 27th Ward in New Orleans on 26 August 1920.

segments.title: Musical family: mother, Frazier and Marrero relatives
segments.summary: His mother played piano and church organ; he explains his kinship to the Marrero and Frazier families, including Lawrence Marrero's father.

segments.title: Teaching himself piano and the nickel parties
segments.summary: His father played a little piano; Williams began at five, learned by watching his mother, never read music, and played nickel house parties.

segments.title: First jobs on drums, Burgundy Street and Club Slipper
segments.summary: He started on drums with an older drummer, played jobs at fifteen on Burgundy Street and at Club Slipper, and recalls the fish-fry and house parties.

segments.chapter: Army service and GI Bill school
segments.title: Army band in Manila and Okinawa
segments.summary: Drafted in 1941, Williams formed a small band in the service, played around Manila and Okinawa, and built the camp himself.

segments.chapter: Army service and GI Bill school
segments.title: Discharge, East St. Louis club and GI Bill music school
segments.summary: After discharge he worked a club in East St. Louis, then attended school on the GI Bill, and they recall other musicians who studied there.

segments.chapter: Working with Coleman and Smiling Joe
segments.title: Freddie Coleman's band at the Mardi Gras lounge and its records
segments.summary: Looking at a photo of the Mardi Gras employees, they identify band members and discuss the records the band made.

segments.chapter: Working with Coleman and Smiling Joe
segments.title: Working with Smiling Joe
segments.summary: Williams worked often with Smiling Joe in town and out of town.

segments.title: Burnell Santiago's piano style and Count Basie
segments.summary: Williams describes Burnell Santiago as a fast-fingered pianist who played blues and everything, and recalls him making Count Basie's band jump.

segments.title: Mitchell and Simon Frazier, Steve Lewis, and missing the older players
segments.summary: They discuss Frazier cousins and Steve Lewis, and Williams says being drafted at 19 or 20 made him miss many older pianists.

segments.title: Udell Wilson and women pianists
segments.summary: Russell asks about Udell Wilson, Emma Barrett, Mrs. Kimble and Mercedes Gorman; Williams doesn't recall them well, and says his mother played little outside church.

segments.title: Whether the pianists sang, and Williams's singing
segments.summary: They ask whether the older pianists sang; Williams says not, and Russell compliments his own singing.

segments.title: Baby Bruce, the party pianist, and the damp-proof piano
segments.summary: Russell and Williams talk about interviewing Baby Bruce and his waterlogged piano, then discuss Williams's own damp-proof piano.

segments.title: Joe and Sam Hopkins playing on Bourbon Street
segments.summary: Williams recalls Joe Hopkins, who plays near Two Sisters on Bourbon Street, and his brother Sam Hopkins.

segments.title: Unrelated CBS TV broadcast on the tape: Armstrong birthday tribute
segments.summary: Recorded television audio with an announcer wishing Louis Armstrong a happy birthday, songs, and a promo for the show Goodbye Again.
